rationale:
bugs_open/259 (resolve by SLUG: '..._one_provision_request_builds_several_billable_gpus'): one provision request built several real, billing Thunder GPUs. Provisioning is PAUSED fleet-wide by owner decision while this is fixed, so this change is what unblocks every lane's GPU access, not just ours.

THE ORIGINAL ROOT CAUSE IN THAT BUG FILE WAS WRONG, AND THIS SUBMISSION CORRECTS IT. It was filed as 'Kafka redelivers while the handler blocks' (synchronous 5-minute handler vs 60s consumer deadlines). Those three code facts are true but do not compose into the cause. What actually happens: the dispatch_provision step carries timeout_seconds 600; when that await expires the chassis retry driver (coordinator.go retryExpiredAwaitedRequest, budget RetryVersion < 3) RE-EXECUTES the step; each execution re-runs DispatchThunderProvisionAction, which mints a NEW request_id (thunder_provision_dispatch.go:99) and publishes a NEW message. Four executions, four billable GPUs. Measured: orchestration 8c5bf926 / correlation 23c9bc6a shows 4 awaited_requests rows, 4 DISTINCT request_ids, 1 orchestration_id, each row processed at EXACTLY its own timeout_at with the next sent ~1s later. Kafka redelivery is DISPROVED, not merely unsupported: a redelivered message replays identical bytes, so request_id would be constant.

This matters for the design, which is why the correction is in the submission and not just the bug file: correlation_id is the ONLY identifier stable across the four attempts. Keying idempotency on request_id — which is what the dispatch code makes look canonical, being per-message, a UUID and the awaited_requests PK — would never fire, and every unit test would pass because a test naturally reuses one id. The bug file's fix candidate 3 (raise KAFKA_SESSION_TIMEOUT / KAFKA_REBALANCE_TIMEOUT) is retired: it addresses a mechanism that is not firing, would cost a build cycle for nothing, and would slow dead-member detection for every consumer sharing that config.

The fix takes a claim keyed on correlation_id BEFORE the vendor call, so a duplicate provision is unrepresentable rather than detected after the money is spent. Reviewers should press hardest on the three judgement calls, which are stated rather than buried: (1) a FAILED attempt keeps its claim — releasing it would restore the exact loop this closes, but it means a transient vendor failure now ends the workflow instead of self-healing; (2) a request with no correlation_id is refused rather than provisioned unguarded; (3) it lives in its own table rather than as a column on thunder_instances, because a pre-create row there would be classified a ghost_row by reconcile_thunder_instances and would file a spurious finding against FTW-042 on every in-flight provision.

This change is ALREADY COMMITTED (forward-only on a shared HEAD; committing is shipping here) but is INERT until a thunder-adapter build and a whole-fleet release the owner runs, and provisioning stays paused until then.

plan.summary: Make provision_instance idempotent on correlation_id via a claim taken before the vendor call, in a new thunder_provision_claims table. A held claim returns ErrProvisionDuplicate, mapped to error_unrecoverable so the chassis cannot retry the thing that builds the second GPU. The claim row doubles as the durable record of a failed provision that bugs_open/258 defect 3 says does not exist.

edits.rationale: The dedup surface. PK on correlation_id IS the mechanism: it makes a duplicate provision unrepresentable rather than detected. Its own table, not a column on thunder_instances, because a pre-create claim row there carries no real vendor id and reconcile_thunder_instances classifies a live row absent at the vendor as a ghost_row (thunder_reconcile_action.go:204-219) — every in-flight provision would file a spurious orphan-sweep finding against FTW-042, which this same lane shipped and got council-approved on 2026-08-09. The claims table has no existing readers, so it perturbs nothing. The verify block INDUCES a duplicate and fails the COMMIT if the constraint accepts it, per the RFC_006 lesson that a block of SELECTs cannot stop a COMMIT.
edits.sketch: CREATE TABLE thunder_provision_claims (correlation_id text PRIMARY KEY, orchestration_id uuid, first_request_id text, training_run_id uuid, requested_by text, attempts integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK (attempts >= 1), status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'claimed' CHECK (status IN ('claimed','created','succeeded','failed')), thunder_instance_id text, provisioning_id uuid, last_error text, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()); -- + DO/RAISE verify that induces a duplicate

edits.rationale: Claim and count in ONE statement. A read-then-insert pair would reintroduce the race the table exists to close — two retry messages arriving close together would both read 'no claim' and both provision. (xmax = 0) is Postgres's own verdict on whether this INSERT inserted or the conflict arm fired, rather than a count we compute and could get wrong. Fails CLOSED: an empty correlation_id, or any infrastructural error, means do-not-provision, because the failure mode this exists to prevent costs real money.
edits.sketch: INSERT INTO thunder_provision_claims (...) VALUES (...) ON CONFLICT (correlation_id) DO UPDATE SET attempts = thunder_provision_claims.attempts + 1 RETURNING correlation_id, attempts, status, thunder_instance_id, provisioning_id, last_error, (xmax = 0) AS inserted;  // !inserted => ErrClaimHeld

edits.rationale: Place the claim between the existing gate checks (cfg.IsPaused, CheckCanProvision) and p.thunderAPI.CreateInstance. The ORDERING is the mechanism: a claim taken after the create leaves the window open exactly where the money is spent. A held claim returns ErrProvisionDuplicate rather than proceeding. Deliberately, a FAILED attempt KEEPS its claim — on 2026-08-12 every attempt failed and the cleanup deleted every box, so if failure released the claim the retry loop would run exactly as before and this fix would be theatre.

CorrelationID/OrchestrationID/RequestID are non-JSON fields set from headers, the same shape as the existing RequestedBy. markClaimFailed records failures on a FRESH context because the parent is often already cancelled on exactly the paths where recording matters most, and it never lets a bookkeeping error mask the real one. This is what supplies bugs_open/258 defect 3's missing audit trail: today a failed provision writes no thunder_instances row and no agent_error_log row, so once pod logs rotate there is nothing left.

CorrelationID string `json:"-"`  // the dedup key; request_id is audit-only, NOT the key
func (p *ProvisionAction) markClaimFailed(ctx context.Context, correlationID, msg string) { recCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second); ... }

edits.rationale: Plumb correlation_id/orchestration_id/request_id from the message headers, and map ErrProvisionDuplicate to a 'provision_duplicate' error code that stays error_unrecoverable. The classification MUST be tested before the isInfrastructureError arm and MUST stay unrecoverable: marking a duplicate refusal recoverable would ask the chassis to retry the very thing that builds the second billable GPU.

Replays the REAL shape — same correlation_id, DIFFERENT request_id, as the retry driver produces. A test reusing the request_id would pass against a broken build, because it would collide on an identifier the real retries never share. Asserts on CREATES AT THE VENDOR, not on rows or errors: the vendor call is the thing that costs money and the only fact bookkeeping cannot fake. PROVEN ABLE TO FAIL: with the refusal branch mutated out it reports 'CreateInstance called 2 times for one logical request'; restored, it passes.

plan.risks: 1) BEHAVIOUR CHANGE for gpu-provisioner, the sole consumer: a second provision_instance under an already-attempted correlation is now REFUSED rather than served. That is the intent, but a workflow relying on the retry driver to re-provision after a transient failure will now fail fast instead of silently spending. Bounded retry (attempts <= N) is the stated next iteration if this proves too strict. 2) A claim row stuck in 'claimed' means the adapter died between claim and create; a later attempt is refused (fails closed) and any box that was built is caught by the FTW-042 orphan sweep — but a human must clear the claim before that correlation can provision again. 3) This does NOT make an a6000 provision succeed: the 600s await vs the adapter's 5-minute waitTimeout is bugs_open/258 defect 2 and is untouched here, so expect the first unpaused run to fail once, cleanly, leaving one claim marked 'failed'. Fixing 258 by RAISING the wait timeout is now safe in a way it was not before, because duplicates can no longer accumulate. 4) Migration 396 must be applied BEFORE the new binary rolls: the adapter treats an absent table as a hard error and refuses to provision. Fails closed, but it will refuse. 5) The bug's co-cause — an adapter error response that does not clear the await (every row processed at its timeout, never at the ~5-min mark when the adapter answered) — is NOT fixed here and is still undiagnosed; it deserves its own 090.
